metadata.title: What Kappa Actually Measures
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning to use and report on AI systems
metadata.fellow: Janvi Chitroda, AI Data Engineer volunteer, Medhavy project, Humanitarians AI
metadata.source: inbox/term2-week05/term2-week5-video-content.md (Week 5); judge model names from inbox/week-01/KEYWORD_QA_PIPELINE_DOCS.md; narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27)
metadata.note: STEM/learning film, hai Plain register on the ai-explainer chassis. Thesis: kappa is agreement corrected for chance — (observed − chance) ÷ (1 − chance) — not accuracy. Worked example: our keyword ensemble, 94.2% raw → Fleiss' kappa 0.49. Formula shown as plain text (no LaTeX). Every on-screen number appears in the Week 5 source as written.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer, ask lands answered. Required intro line + AI-narration disclosure.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Janvi and this video is about kappa: how to tell whether judges agree more than chance would predict. This narration is an AI-generated voice; the work is mine.

props.command: My three judges agree 94.2% of the time. How do I tell how much of that is more than chance?
output: Estimate chance from each tag's share

beats.role_note: Two judge cards 'judge A · not reading' / 'judge B · not reading'; a row of items where most share one tag; an agreement bar rises (illustration, no numbers); caption 'raw agreement can't tell the difference'.
beats.narration_text: Imagine two judges who tag items without reading them. If most items get the same tag anyway, these judges will still agree often. Raw agreement can't tell that apart from real agreement.
beats.visual_intent: Two judge cards 'judge A · not reading' / 'judge B · not reading'; a row of items where most share one tag; an agreement bar rises (illustration, no numbers); caption 'raw agreement can't tell the difference'.

beats.role_note: Plain-text formula card 'kappa = (observed − chance) ÷ (1 − chance)' built term by term; scale 0 = chance … 1 = perfect.
beats.narration_text: Kappa fixes this. Take the observed agreement, subtract the agreement you'd expect by chance, and divide by the most you could have gained over chance. Zero means no better than chance. One means perfect agreement.
beats.visual_intent: Plain-text formula card 'kappa = (observed − chance) ÷ (1 − chance)' built term by term; scale 0 = chance … 1 = perfect.

beats.role_note: Segmented base-rate bar (Week 1 B04 triage bar style): approved 45.0% · supplementary 33.0% · too_basic 11.9% · junk 10.2%; chip 'chance ≈ 67%'.
beats.narration_text: Chance depends on the base rates. In our keyword data, 45 percent of all tags were approved and 33 percent supplementary. With a mix that skewed, chance agreement is about 67 percent.
beats.visual_intent: Segmented base-rate bar (Week 1 B04 triage bar style): approved 45.0% · supplementary 33.0% · too_basic 11.9% · junk 10.2%; chip 'chance ≈ 67%'.

beats.role_note: '94.2% raw agreement' → 'Fleiss' kappa 0.49'; chips 'Fleiss: three or more raters at once' · 'Cohen: one pair at a time'.
beats.narration_text: That's why our 94.2 percent raw agreement became a Fleiss' kappa of 0.49. Fleiss' kappa handles three or more raters at once; Cohen's kappa compares one pair at a time.
beats.visual_intent: '94.2% raw agreement' → 'Fleiss' kappa 0.49'; chips 'Fleiss: three or more raters at once' · 'Cohen: one pair at a time'.

beats.role_note: Pairwise table with ink logos: Mistral–Claude 0.6559 · Mistral–GPT-4o-mini 0.4251 · GPT-4o-mini–Claude 0.4022 (exact source values).
beats.narration_text: Pairwise kappa tells you who agrees with whom. In our data, Mistral and Claude reached 0.66, while each pair with G P T four o mini was near 0.4.
beats.visual_intent: Pairwise table with ink logos: Mistral–Claude 0.6559 · Mistral–GPT-4o-mini 0.4251 · GPT-4o-mini–Claude 0.4022 (exact source values).

beats.role_note: 'kappa: agreement, corrected for chance — not accuracy'; three judge logos → one shared answer card 'the same mistake' → 'kappa: still high'; caption 'moderate, substantial: conventions, not laws'.
beats.narration_text: What kappa doesn't tell you is whether anyone is right. It's still agreement, just corrected for chance. Three judges can share the same mistake and still score high. And labels like moderate or substantial are conventions, not laws.
beats.visual_intent: 'kappa: agreement, corrected for chance — not accuracy'; three judge logos → one shared answer card 'the same mistake' → 'kappa: still high'; caption 'moderate, substantial: conventions, not laws'.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed in the composer.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take two sets of labels from any two raters. Count how often they agree, then estimate chance from each label's share, and see how much of the agreement is left.
